Apply Benjamini-Hochberg FDR; do not report nominal p-values as significant findings.
State the pre-filtering rule and the number of genes retained out of 12,000.

steps.description: Run DESeq2 on all 12 samples using the aligned matrix from T1S1 with design ~condition, chow/control as the reference level. steps.name: Leave-one-out sensitivity to the shallow sample
caveats: Dropping one sample from an n=6 group reduces power and will typically shrink the significant-gene list even when the underlying signal is identical — the log2FC concordance, not the hit count, is the robustness measure.

steps.context: sample_01 is ~4x shallower than the median. Rather than deciding a priori to keep or drop it, this step measures the actual consequence of the choice, which is the defensible way to answer the user's 'one sample looks shallow' concern. Note that removing sample_01 leaves an unbalanced 6 vs 5 (or 5 vs 6) design, which itself costs power — some loss of significant genes is expected from n alone and must not be misread as instability.
steps.question: How much does the high-fat-diet vs chow gene list depend on the shallow sample_01 — does dropping it change which genes are called significant?
constraints: Change exactly one thing relative to T1S2 — the removal of sample_01. Design, filtering, shrinkage method and FDR threshold must be identical.
Report which condition group sample_01 belongs to and the resulting group sizes after exclusion.
Do not present the leave-one-out run as the primary result unless T1S1 found sample_01 to be a genuine expression outlier; if so, say explicitly that the primary designation changed and why.
Attribute any drop in significant-gene count between runs to power loss versus instability using the log2FC concordance, not by count comparison alone.
steps.description: Re-run the identical DESeq2 pipeline from T1S2 (same design, same pre-filtering rule, same shrinkage and FDR settings) on the 11 samples remaining after excluding sample_01, and compare directly to the 12-sample primary result. Explicit lists of genes gained and lost between the runs.
A one-paragraph verdict on robustness that distinguishes power loss from result instability.

GSEA permutation p-values on a 12-sample gene-level ranking are approximate; treat borderline sets accordingly.

GSEA on the full ranked list is preferred over threshold-based over-representation because with n=6 per group the significant-gene list may be small; the ORA cross-check is secondary.

constraints: Use the MOUSE hallmark collection (MGI symbols). Using the human hallmark GMT on these mouse symbols would silently produce near-empty overlaps and meaningless results — verify the organism of the resolved gene-set file and abort with a clear message if only a human collection is available.
Rank genes once, using the T1S2 ranking statistic; do not re-rank by a different metric between the GSEA and any reported plots.
Set a random seed and report it, so the permutation-based p-values are reproducible.
Report BH-adjusted p-values across the hallmark sets tested and state the number of sets tested.
Report the symbol-overlap fraction between the ranked list and the hallmark collection before interpreting any enrichment.
If no hallmark set reaches padj < 0.05, report the top sets by NES clearly marked as not significant — do not switch to nominal p-values as the headline.
steps.description: Run pre-ranked GSEA (fgsea) on the full ranked gene list from T1S2 against the mouse hallmark gene set collection — the MSigDB hallmark sets for Mus musculus with MGI gene symbols, which the environment stages as a GMT and which matches the identifier space of counts.csv directly, so no ortholog mapping is required. plan.title: HFD vs chow mouse liver DE + hallmark GSEA
plan.analytical_narrative:
The input is a single-batch bulk RNA-seq experiment: gene-level Salmon counts for 12,000 mouse gene symbols across 12 liver samples (counts.csv, 12000 x 13 — one gene-id column plus 12 sample columns), with metadata.csv giving one condition label per sample (6 high-fat diet vs 6 chow, unpaired). The research question has two halves — which genes change, and which hallmark pathways change — plus one explicit data concern: sample_01 has a library size roughly 4x below the median.

The shallow sample is handled first and empirically rather than by assumption. Library size alone is not grounds for exclusion: DESeq2's median-of-ratios normalization and the negative-binomial fit absorb depth differences, and a 4x lower depth on a 12-sample design mainly costs precision for low-count genes in that one sample. T1S1 therefore quantifies the problem — per-sample library sizes, detected-gene counts, size factors, PCA on VST values, and sample-sample correlation — and decides on evidence whether sample_01 is merely shallow (keep) or also an expression outlier (a candidate for a sensitivity analysis). Critically, the decision is not allowed to silently change the primary result: T1S2 runs the full 6v6 DESeq2 contrast, and T1S3 re-runs the identical contrast leaving sample_01 out, so the reported gene list is accompanied by a concrete statement of how much it depends on that one sample. That is the honest answer to 'one sample looks shallow'.

DESeq2 (R, 1.52.0) is used rather than a simpler test because n=6 per group is small and the shrinkage of dispersion and of log-fold-changes is what makes the effect sizes interpretable at this sample size. The counts are Salmon-derived and the profile explicitly does not record whether a length/offset correction was applied; the step must therefore treat them as a plain integer count matrix, round if non-integer, and state that assumption — it must not invent a tximport offset it does not have.

Pathway analysis uses GSEA on the full DESeq2-ranked gene list rather than over-representation on a thresholded list, because with 12 samples the significant-gene set may be small and a rank-based test uses the whole signal. The mouse hallmark collection is staged in the reference store (MSigDB 2026.1, MGI symbols), which matches the organism and the identifier space of the counts exactly — no human-to-mouse ortholog mapping is needed, and using the human hallmark file here would be an error. T1S4 also reports the fraction of counts.csv symbols that match the GMT, since 12,000 genes is a reduced feature space and low overlap would undermine the enrichment result.
